#Text=Low retention of restocked laboratory_reared long_spined sea urchinsÊDiadema antillarumÊdue to Spanish hogfishÊBodianus rufusÊpredation.

#Text=Tom Wijers,ÊOliver Klokman,ÊAlbertinka J Murk,ÊJilles Sijbrandij,ÊAlwin Hylkema First published: 12 September 2024 Ê https://doi.org/10.1111/rec.14264 Author contributions: OK, JS, AH conceived and designed the research; OK, JS, AH performed the experiments; TW, OK, JS, AH analyzed the data; TW, OK, AJM, JS, AH wrote and edited the manuscript; OK, TW contributed equally to this study.

#Text=Abstract.
#Text=The die_off of the long_spined sea urchin Diadema antillarumÊin the 1980s highlighted its crucial role as a primary grazer in tropical western Atlantic coral reefs.
#Text=However, natural recovery has been slow, exacerbated by a new die_off in 2022.
#Text=Interest in actively restoringÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊpopulations has grown with the emergence of culture and rearing techniques.
#Text=Restocking reefs with laboratory_reared urchins shows potential for enhancing coral reef resilience by reducing algal cover and promoting coral settlement, but success rates vary.
#Text=Predation and migration contribute to low retention rates, with distinguishing between them is challenging.
#Text=In this study near Saba, Caribbean Netherlands, we released 200 laboratory_rearedÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊon a reef and monitored forÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊretention and potentialÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊpredator presence and interaction for 35 days.
#Text=Only 40% of the urchins were still present on the reef after day one.
#Text=The Spanish hogfishÊBodianus rufusÊwas identified as the primary daytime predator, responsible for nine direct predation events.
#Text=No nighttime predation was observed, but interaction with a batwing coral crabÊCarpilius corallinusÊwas noted.
#Text=These insights can help optimize future restocking attempts and emphasizeÊthe importance of assessing predator presence beforehand.
#Text=Reefs with high abundances of predators such as Spanish hogfish should be avoided forÊD antillarumÊrestocking.
#Text=In addition, before being released, lab_reared animals should be given time to acclimate to conditions in the wild by being placed in protected in situ cages.
#Text=Here, they could also grow to larger sizes that are less vulnerable to predation.
#Text=Implications for Practice * Site selection based on predation pressure and shelter availability could increase retention of restockedÊDiadema antillarum.
#Text=Sites with high Spanish hogfish or queen triggerfish abundances should be avoided unless temporal predator control is possible.
#Text=* Scaling up larval culture techniques and juvenile rearing methods are necessary to effectively restoreÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊpopulations with a significant impact on a local and regional scale.
#Text=* Laboratory_reared sea urchins should be acclimated in a protected semi_natural environment before restocking to increase survival.
#Text=*
#Text=Further studies are needed to determine the optimalÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊsize for restocking to maximize survival and minimize resource use.
#Text=Introduction.

#Text=Human activities have clearly influenced coral reef ecosystems for centuries, primarily through overfishing, destructive fishing methods, direct reef damage, and the introduction of pollutants (Pandolfi et alÊ2003).

#Text=These anthropogenic factors have led to a pronounced reduction in coral cover, diminished biodiversity, and the deterioration of the essential structural characteristics provided by coral reefs (Eddy et alÊ2021).

#Text=Particularly, tropical western Atlantic coral reefs have experienced substantial and enduring degradation (Mumby et alÊ2007), with a marked decrease in coral cover in recent decades (Jackson et alÊ2014).

#Text=This decline has been further exacerbated by additional stressors, including the impacts of hurricanes, the proliferation of coral diseases (Aronson & PrechtÊ2001; Precht et alÊ2016), climate change induced coral bleaching events (Sully et alÊ2019), and the extensive mortality of a keystone herbivore species, the long_spined sea urchinÊDiadema antillarumÊin
#Text=the 1980s (Lessios et alÊ1984).
#Text=In the absence of grazing byÊD.

#Text=antillarum, turf algae, and macroalgae cover increased on the majority of coral reefs (CarpenterÊ1986; Hughes et alÊ1987; LessiosÊ1988), inhibiting recruitment and leaving the reefs in a coral degraded state (MumbyÊ2009).
#Text=Since the mass mortality in the 1980s, the recovery ofÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊhas been slow, with an average of 12% over a span of 30 years (LessiosÊ2016).
#Text=On reefs whereÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊpopulations have recovered, algae cover was reduced, and coral recruitment increased (Aronson & PrechtÊ2000; Idjadi et alÊ2010), underscoring the critical significance ofÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊin the recovery of Caribbean reefs.

#Text=Several restoration methods, such as restocking (Chiappone et alÊ2003; Macia et alÊ2007; WilliamsÊ2022) and assisted natural recovery (Hylkema et alÊ2022), have the potential to accelerate the pace ofÊD. antillarumÊrecovery.
#Text=Restocking can be done with culturedÊD.

#Text=antillarumÊ(Pilnick et alÊ2022; Wijers et alÊ2023) or collected settlers reared in tanks (WilliamsÊ2018,Ê2022; de Breuyn et alÊ2023), but has mostly been done by translocating individuals from recovered populations to experimental plots (Nedimyer & MoeÊ2006; de Breuyn et alÊ2023; Pilnick et alÊ2023).
#Text=Some studies show encouraging results, with positive effects on the reefs after restocking withÊD.
#Text=antillarum.
#Text=Chiappone et al (2003) translocated a total of 693 juvenileÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊwith 30% retention after 1 year.
#Text=This resulted in a reduced cover of brown foliose algae and an increase in coverage of stony corals and crustose coralline algae.
#Text=Similarly, Macia et al (2007) showed a decrease in macroalgae and an increase in the amount of bare space after translocating 508ÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊwith 26% retention after 6 months.
#Text=Unfortunately, not all attempts to restock populations are successful, frequently demonstrating suboptimal retention rates over extended periods.
#Text=This is primarily ascribed to predation (The Nature ConservancyÊ2004), migration away from the reef (WilliamsÊ2018), or a combination of both (DameÊ2008; WilliamsÊ2022; de Breuyn et alÊ2023).
#Text=In addition, when a reef ecosystem lacks the requisite shelter space (Macia et alÊ2007; BurdickÊ2008; Bodmer et alÊ2021),ÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊare more inclined to migrate, which makes them more vulnerable to predation (CarpenterÊ1984).
#Text=Given that these factors often interact and overlap, distinguishing their individual contributions can prove challenging.

#Text=To determine the main factor that reduces retention, a high frequency of observations during both day and nighttime is needed, which has not been done in previous studies (BurdickÊ2008; WilliamsÊ2022; de Breuyn et alÊ2023).
#Text=In this study, a restocking experiment was conducted near the island of Saba, Caribbean Netherlands.
#Text=Laboratory_rearedÊD antillarumÊwere released onto a patch reef and closely monitored for retention, migration, and predation during a period of 5 weeks.

#Text=In the first week both daytime and nighttime monitoring dives were conducted alongside the deployment of cameras, resulting in 15 hours of diver observations and over 28 hours of time_lapse camera footage.
#Text=Instances of predation, as well as potential predation attempts on the releasedÊD antillarumÊwere documented and are presented here.
#Text=The findings presented in this study offer valuable insights into the challenges associated withÊD antillarumÊrestocking.
#Text=These insights are instrumental in guiding future proactive interventions aimed at fostering positive effects on reef ecosystems.
#Text=Methods.

#Text=Experimental Setup Diadema antillarumÊRearing In total 200 juvenileÊDiadema antillarumÊsea urchins were reared for the restocking experiment, for 30% originating from larval cultivation and for 70% from settlers collected from the wild.
#Text=In June 2022, larval cultivation took place on Saba, Caribbean Netherlands, following the methods outlined by Wijers et al (2023).
#Text=Concurrently, between April and June 2022, wild settlers were gathered in proximity to the Saban reefs, following Hylkema et al (2022).
#Text=AllÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊwere subsequently reared in 76_L rectangular recirculation tanks for 6_9 months.

#Text=To provide suitable habitat conditions, each tank was equipped with two halves of a 12 cm diameter flower pot and two fist_sized volcanic rocks, offering rugosity and hiding spaces, as these factors could potentially influence shelter behavior (Sharp et alÊ2018,Ê2023).
#Text=During the initial 2 months of rearing, a maximum of 50 urchins were maintained in each tank, which was subsequently reduced to a maximum of 20 urchins per tank.
#Text=Within these open polypropylene tanks, filtration, and water circulation was provided by airlift sponge filters.
#Text=Artificial lighting was employed using one Phillips 23w 1,600 lm fluorescent bulb per tank with a 12_hour light and 12_hour dark photoperiod.
#Text=Weekly maintenance included salinity adjustment, the removal of debris from the tank bottoms, followed by a 20% water change.

#Text=As the juveniles were partly reared during the 2022 Caribbean_wideÊD. antillarumÊdie_off (Hylkema et alÊ2023), tank refreshes were completed using artificial sea water (Tropic Marin salt REEF_MIX) on full strength (35 g/L) during this mortality period and natural sea water was used again from November 2022 onwards, when population recovery was observed on local reefs.
#Text=JuvenileÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊwere fed thoroughly rinsed macro algae, collected from nearby reefs, and grazer pellets until saturated.
#Text=Nutrients (NO3, NO4, PO4) were tested weekly, and daily temperature fluctuated between 26 and 28 degrees C. Two days before release, the mean test size (body without spines) of the rearedÊD.
#Text=antillarumwas determined to be 15.8 +/_

#Text=Reef Description

#Text=The experimental restocking reef was located at Wells Bay at the dive site Torrens Point (17.642637 degrees N, 063.254648 degrees W) and measured approximately 25 m in length and 6 m in width (FigÊ1).
#Text=The reef was situated at a depth of 9 m sloping down to a depth of 11 m at the side and featured a nearly 90 degrees incline leading down to the sand substrate located 1.5_2 m below.

#Text=For the purpose of this study, the reef was subdivided into four quadrants (FigÊ1) that were treated as independent replicates, as no movement of urchins between quadrants was observed and to make a clear division for divers/stationary camera observations.
#Text=The size of the four replicate quadrants was defined, taking into account that one team or camera would be able to finalize a full monitoring per time point.
#Text=Ideally, four reefs of similar size and proximity would have been used as replicates, but this was not feasible due to limited resources.
#Text=The border of each quadrant was clearly marked with orange rope, to avoid overlapping observations or counts.
#Text=The reef had substantial structural complexity, providing sufficient crevices as hiding space for the restockedÊD.

#Text=Roving Diver Survey To assess the presence of potential predators, also on the adjacent reefs, a roving diver visual survey was conducted on day 14 at 9:00 hours.
#Text=This survey was adapted from the fish roving diver technique (Hill & WilkinsonÊ2004) and involved gathering presence/absence data as well as frequency information.
#Text=In this study, we specifically focused on fishes identified as potential predators.
#Text=In short, two divers systematically inspected the reef areas extending 250 m northward and 250 m eastward from this starting point, dedicating 30 minutes to the survey.
#Text=During this time the presence and sizes were documented of all potential predators ofÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊin the larger region of interest around and including the test reef area.
#Text=The survey was conducted following a zigzag pattern, with divers scanning an area extending up to 10 m in all directions to ensure the inclusion of more elusive species.

#Text=Divers maintained a slow and consistent pace, trying to traverse hard substrate areas when sand patches were encountered, and actively searched for fish sheltering underneath ledges or within caves, among other potential hiding places.

#Text=Stationary Camera Observations To assess predation and predator presence on the reef, especially when divers are not present, stationary cameras (GoPro Hero 8 Black) were deployed on days 0, 1, and 3 of the experiment.
#Text=Four cameras were installed on temporary frames, with one camera for each quadrant of the experimental reef.

#Text=The stationary cameras took photos every 5 seconds, day (starting at 11:00 hours) and night (starting at 18:00 hours).

#Text=Discussion.
#Text=Overall retention of restockedÊDiadema antillarumÊin
#Text=this research was low, with less than 5% of the urchins recovered after 9 days and only two of a total of 200 after 35 days.
#Text=Spanish hogfish were identified as the main diurnal predator, with nine successful attacks recorded through a combination of stationary cameras and diver observations.
#Text=One interaction with a batwing coral crab was observed during the night, though no successful attack were recorded.
#Text=This strongly suggests daytime predation as the primary factor contributing to the low retention rate and is strengthened by the fact that no migration off the experimental reef was observed.
#Text=The decline in retention found in this research was steeper compared to de Breuyn et al (2023), who still had over 25% retention, with both wild and laboratory_rearedÊD.
#Text=antillarum, 10 days after restocking.
#Text=They releasedÊD.
#Text=antillarumÊon small artificial reefs, providing shelter, which might explain the higher retention compared to our findings.
#Text=ÊD.
#Text=antillarumshelter during daylight hours, emerging from their hiding spots during the night (Randall et alÊ1964; Behrents et alÊ1984).
#Text=Even though the reef seemed to have sufficient hiding space for theÊD.

#Text=The observed instances of predation during the daytime indicate that the hiding spaces available may not have been sufficiently effective, or released lab_cultured individuals did not have sufficient awareness or time to establish where adequate shelter may be found.
